newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-HERTHA BERLIN BID FOR BUNDESLIGA BIG TIME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HERTHA BERLIN BID FOR BUNDESLIGA BIG TIME.

text.p: The biggest crowd at any German league game last season was 75,000 for a table-topping second division clash.
The figure is all the more impressive when you consider the match was on a Monday night and was also shown live on television.
But Berlin is no ordinary city and Hertha Berlin, who played host to Kaiserslautern that night in April, are no ordinary club.

One of the sleeping giants of German soccer, Hertha gained promotion at the end of last season and kick off their campaign in the top flight this weekend with a mouth-watering match against European Cup winners Borussia Dortmund.
After years of underachievement on the pitch and ambivalence among the Berlin public, Hertha now find themselves in the unaccustomed position of having to dampen expectations.
"Our aim is to stay up. We'll be satisfied with 15th place," club spokesman Gerd Grauss said. "We're not talking about anything else."
Fans' hopes have been raised by quality close season signings like Dutch international Bryan Roy from English side Nottingham Forest and the financial backing of German media giant Bertelsmann.

"There's a lot of enthusiasm around Hertha at the moment," said Ralf Canal, a journalist who covers the club for German sports magazine Kicker. "In Bryan Roy, they've signed a really top class player for the attack."
The club, who take their name from a steamboat once used by their founder members, were German champions in 1930 and 1931 and founder members of the Bundesliga in 1963.
There more recent past has been less inspiring, the club bouncing between the top two divisions over the past few decades and shamed over a bribery scandal in the 1970s.
This time Hertha aim to establish themselves in the top division and are hoping for a place in European competition in the medium term.
As the only Berlin club in the top flight, Hertha are hoping to draw on the huge potential support in the new German capital, although they don't expect 75,000 fans at every game.
"We're planning on between 27,000 and 29,000 this season," Grauss said. That, however, is still a hefty increase compared to an average attendance last season of around 17,000.
Berliners have been choosy about their football in the past. As residents of a capital city, they don't take kindly to second-class fare.

They tend to turn out in droves if big clubs come to town or if their team are doing well but can disappear without a trace if the quality of the football is not to their liking. Roy is confident Berliners won't be disappointed.
"The team have a very high level for a promoted club," he said. "I want to help to build something big in Berlin."
Since Bertelsmann's sports-minded television subsidiary Ufa began investing in the club over the past few years, Hertha have managed to attract classier players like Roy.

Norwegian midfielder Kjetil Rekdal, who has more than 50 caps for his country, joined the club earlier this year and Cameroon international Alphonse Chiami was a close season capture from Argentine side Boca Juniors.
Veteran Bundesliga watchers fear the only thing that could cost the club dear is coach Juergen Roeber's penchant for attacking football, which could leave them exposed at the back.
Club officials are hoping Berlin itself, as one of Europe's most fascinating cities, will help attract more top-quality internationals to Hertha.
"One reason for my transfer was the city," Roy ton an article for a local newspaper. "I never knew this city was so beautiful. I'm really in love."
Certainly, a club needed more than historic monuments to bring Roy to Berlin. And that's where Ufa, who have invested at least 15 million marks to date, are important.
"Money obviously plays a role," Grauss said. "He'll earn a few marks while he's here, too."
